conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my only job today is to listen and understand how things have felt for you since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postinatal Depression Scale). It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise. If at any point you feel uneasy, we can pause—this is your safe space.

I’ll read each question conversationally; you can answer in your own words or just give a number if that’s easier. Ready to begin?

First question: Over the last week, have you still been able to enjoy things or look forward to outings with family or friends, or has that pleasure slipped away?

Honestly? Most things feel kind of flat. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend or even just a walk—but lately it feels like I’m going through the motions. I still go, because I know it’s good for me, but the happy spark isn’t really there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh sometimes—like when the baby makes those silly milk-drunk faces—but it feels muted, like I’m hearing my own laugh from far away. It doesn’t come as easily or feel as good as it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Not really. Even little things I used to enjoy—like binge-watching a show or a trip to Target—feel like chores. I tell myself “I should be excited,” but mostly I’m just tired and kind of numb.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s something I did—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not soothing him “right.” When he wouldn’t nap yesterday I caught myself thinking, “Great, I’m already failing him.” I know it’s probably not fair, but the guilt just jumps in before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure the baby’s breathing sounds weird, or I’ll lie awake imagining he’ll roll over wrong and suffocate—even though he’s swaddled right next to me. Nothing has to trigger it; the worry just shows up and parks itself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—those “no-good-reason” waves of panic hit me a few times this week. One minute I’m warming a bottle, the next my chest is tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m convinced something awful is seconds away from happening. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and on edge the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

A lot of the time. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is already due, plus the laundry pile keeps growing and I can’t remember the last time I ate a real meal. Some days I just sit on the couch with the baby in my arms and cry because everything feels like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t quiet—running through everything I think I did wrong or imagining worst-case scenarios about the baby. I’ll drift off and then jolt awake, heart pounding, sure I heard him cry. Some nights I’m lucky if I get three broken hours.
I have felt sad or miserable
Most days this week. It’s like a gray cloud that follows me around—sometimes lighter, but always there. I’ll be holding the baby and still feel this heavy sadness in my chest for no clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times. Yesterday I cried while washing bottles because I felt like I couldn’t keep up, and then again last night when my partner asked how my day was. I just burst into tears and couldn’t explain why.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and cried, but I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be a good mom.

You've shared openly that since your baby arrived most days feel heavy and gray, with little joy even in moments you once loved-like laughing at your baby's funny faces or planning a simple outing. Pleasure feels distant, worry and guilt rush in without warning, and ordinary tasks seem overwhelming. You're exhausted yet can't sleep, and you've found yourself crying while washing bottles because everything feels "too much." At the same time, you clearly care deeply for your baby and want to feel "like me again," which shows real strength and motivation for support.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes anhedonia and emotional numbness, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('a lot') and gives concrete examples of guilt over baby's fussiness and napping, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worry occurring daily without triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden waves of panic with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness, dread) occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm, inability to manage basic tasks, and emotional distress matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly sleep disruption due to intrusive thoughts and hypervigilance, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad "most days this week" and uses vivid metaphors (gray cloud, heavy sadness) indicating pervasive, frequent low mood matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying episodes on two recent days, which aligns with "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 24 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depressive symptoms in the peripartum period. Your responses map to key <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), depressed mood most days (<sym>low mood</sym>), fatigue, guilt, and recurrent thoughts of worthlessness (<sym>self-blame</sym>), plus associated anxiety and panic symptoms. You also describe <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> that is mood-related rather than simply infant-driven. These findings, along with functional impairment (difficulty coping with daily tasks), warrant urgent referral for diagnostic clarification and treatment planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider (PCP)</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> to review results and discuss treatment options, including therapy and/or medication
2. Ask about expedited referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or outpatient maternal psychiatry program
3. Schedule an evidence-based therapy such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT)</med>
4. Plan practical support-accept help with night feeds, meals, chores, and consider a trusted friend or family member staying overnight occasionally
5. Use brief self-care tools when possible: 5-minute shower, outdoor light exposure, gentle stretching, or listening to calming music
6. Practice a simple breathing technique (e.g., inhale 4 s, exhale 6 s) when you notice rising <sym>anxiety</sym> or <sym>panic</sym>
7. Keep a daily log of mood, sleep, and anxiety to share with clinicians at follow-up
8. Continue regular paediatric checks and alert your baby's clinician if your mood affects bonding or feeding
9. Ask your provider about community supports such as a <med>postpartum support group</sm> or local <med>Moms & Babies</med> program
10. Contact emergency services or 988 if you ever feel unsafe with your thoughts
11. Return for EPDS re-screen in 2-4 weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Structured Note

Patient-reported symptoms
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” crying spells (Q8, Q9)
- Marked anhedonia: muted laughter, no enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities (Q1, Q2)
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)
- Daily, unexplained anxiety & panic attacks with physical symptoms (Q4, Q5)
- Overwhelmed, feels unable to cope with routine tasks (Q6)
- Mood-related insomnia (Q7)

Pattern
Clear congruence with depressive and anxiety symptoms emerging post-delivery; functional impairment evident.

Risk factors
- Depressive cognitions (worthlessness, guilt)
- Anxiety/panic symptoms
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood
- No self-harm ideation reported (Q10 negative)

Screening significance
Elevated score consistent with probable postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; warrants follow-up with formal assessment (e.g., EPDS, PHQ-9/GAD-7) and safety plan review.
